--- title: "Continuous-time Markov chains and jump processes" course-unit: ch05-jump-processes status: complete --- ## Where we are | Model | Determinism | Time | State | |---|---|---|---| | ODE (Day 1) | deterministic | continuous | continuous | | Function map (Day 1) | deterministic | discrete | continuous | | Markov chain (Day 1) | stochastic | discrete | discrete | | **Jump process (now)** | **stochastic** | **continuous** | **discrete** | All four are population models: the state is counts, not people. ::: {.notes} Two minutes at the start of the day. These four axes are the map the whole course is drawn on, and today fills in the last population-level corner: stochastic, continuous in time, discrete in state. Point out that the individual-level column is still empty; that is Day 3. ::: ## Why events matter - A CTMC waits for the next infection or recovery. - The state is integer-valued: $X=(S,I,R)$. - Exact event timing exposes fade-out and peak variability. For the baseline population, $$ a_{\mathrm{inf}}=\frac{\beta cSI}{N},\qquad a_{\mathrm{rec}}=\gamma I. $$ ::: {.notes} Contrast this with an ODE: an ODE advances all flows over a numerical interval, while a jump process samples the next event and its type. ::: ## Recap: where the exponential comes from An event with constant hazard $r$ has waiting time $T$ with $$ \Pr(T>t)=e^{-rt},\qquad \Pr(T\le\delta t)=1-e^{-r\delta t}, $$ the same conversion used for the discrete-time chain on Day 1. ::: {.notes} Five minutes, no derivation on the board. Point out that the survival function is where yesterday's rate-to-proportion rule came from: the per-step probability is the chance the waiting time lands inside the step. The full derivation is in the probability prerequisite; nobody needs to have read it to follow this session. ::: ## Recap: memoryless clocks and which one rings first Exponential waiting times are **memoryless**, $$ \Pr(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-rt}=\Pr(T>t), $$ so no per-individual clock has to be carried and the counts $(S,I,R)$ are the whole state. With competing events at rates $a_j$ and $a_0=\sum_j a_j$, $$ \min_j T_j\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0), \qquad \Pr(J=j)=\frac{a_j}{a_0}. $$ ::: {.notes} Memorylessness is a real assumption about the disease: someone infectious for a week is no closer to recovering than someone infected this morning. The two displayed results are the whole Gillespie algorithm: when the next event happens, and which one it is. The next slide is bookkeeping rather than new mathematics. Learners who want the derivations should read the waiting-times section of the probability prerequisite afterwards. ::: ## Gillespie direct algorithm At state $x$, let $a_0=a_{\mathrm{inf}}+a_{\mathrm{rec}}$. 1. Draw $\tau\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0)$. 2. Choose infection with probability $a_{\mathrm{inf}}/a_0$. 3. Apply $(-1,+1,0)$ or $(0,-1,+1)$. This is a stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, population-level model. Every event conserves $S+I+R=N$. ::: {.notes} The propensities are rates, not probabilities. The waiting time is continuous even though the state changes by integer increments. ::: ## A visible Julia kernel {.smaller} ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Random, StableRNGs function gillespie_sir(N, I₀, β, c, γ, tmax, rng) t, x = 0.0, [N - I₀, I₀, 0] times, states = [t], [copy(x)] while t < tmax && x[2] > 0 a = (β*c*x[1]*x[2]/N, γ*x[2]) a₀ = sum(a) a₀ == 0 && break t += randexp(rng)/a₀ t > tmax && break if rand(rng)*a₀ < a[1] x[1] -= 1; x[2] += 1 else x[2] -= 1; x[3] += 1 end push!(times, t); push!(states, copy(x)) end (; times, states) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` gillespie_sir (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} The state update is the stoichiometric change vector in code. The local StableRNG makes the result reproducible without relying on global state. ::: ## One path, and the ODE through it {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch04-path .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch04-path .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One exact CTMC path (steps) against the mean-field ODE (dashed). ::: ::: ::: {.notes} This is the picture the whole morning is about. Every wiggle is a real event, and at a thousand people there are well over a thousand of them, so the steps merge into a rough curve. Zooming in on the first few days is where you would see individual jumps. The dashed curves are yesterday's model, and the gap is not solver error: this particular realization ran a few days late, and a different seed would run early. The title numbers are generated at render time and are realization-specific; conservation is asserted, so a broken kernel would fail the render. Do not let anyone read one path as an expected epidemic; that is the next two slides. ::: ## Recap: two kinds of spread For $M$ independent paths with summary values $z_1,\dots,z_M$, $$ \bar z=\frac1M\sum_k z_k,\qquad s^2=\frac1{M-1}\sum_k (z_k-\bar z)^2,\qquad \operatorname{se}(\bar z)=\frac{s}{\sqrt M}. $$ - The standard deviation $s$ describes **the epidemics**: how much peak size varies. More simulation does not shrink it. - The standard error $\operatorname{se}(\bar z)$ describes **our estimate** of the average, and does shrink, as $1/\sqrt M$: four times the work to halve it. ::: {.notes} Three minutes, and it pays for itself four times today. These two spreads get confused constantly, so keep them apart: one is a property of the disease process, the other a property of how hard we simulated. Say explicitly that this is the vocabulary the rest of the day uses. The relative spread of SDE peaks after the break, the variance-to-mean ratio of case counts this afternoon, and the variance decomposition in the last session all live on this slide. Nobody needs the probability prerequisite for it. ::: ## Three ways to write one model {.smaller} The model has not changed since the last slide. Only the *notation* changes. | | what you write | who writes the code | |---|---|---| | **Day 1** | a function: every term, by hand | you | | **Today** | a macro: the model as stated | the library | A hand-written function works in any language, and that is its virtue. It is also longer than the mathematics it encodes, and every extra line is somewhere a sign can go wrong. Macros let Julia read the model the way it is written on paper and generate the loop for you — which is what makes a fifty-compartment model tractable. Two toolkits do this in SciML, and today uses both: **ModelingToolkit.jl** and **Catalyst.jl**. ::: {.notes} This is the framing slide for the rest of the day, so do not rush it. The point is not that macros are clever; it is that all three representations are the same process. The hand-written kernel earlier was deliberately the Day 1 style: it could have been C or R, and you had to be the one who got the stoichiometry right. Everything from here on states the model and lets the library write the loop. Stress that this is a claim we are about to check, not a promise. ::: ## The ODE, by hand and by declaration {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Day 1: a kernel you write. ::: {#cell-ch04-hand-ode .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t) S, I, R = u κ, γ = p du[1] = -κ*S*I du[2] = κ*S*I - γ*I du[3] = γ*I return nothing end ``` ::: {#ch04-hand-ode .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` sir_ode! (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Today: the equations, stated. ::: {#cell-ch04-mtk-ode .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using ModelingToolkit using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D @parameters κ γ @variables S(t) I(t) R(t) @named odesys = System( [D(S) ~ -κ*S*I, D(I) ~ κ*S*I - γ*I, D(R) ~ γ*I], t) ``` ::: {#ch04-mtk-ode .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Unknowns (3): see unknowns(odesys)

  I(t)
  R(t)
Parameters (2): see parameters(odesys)

``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: Three assignments into a `du` vector you must index correctly, against three named equations. Day 1 wrote this with $\beta$, $c$ and $N$; here $\kappa=\beta c/N$ throughout. ::: {.notes} Put the two columns up and let them look before saying anything. The left is exactly what we did yesterday and it is not bad code — it is fast, it is explicit, and you could hand it to a C programmer. What it is not is the mathematics: `du[2]` is the infectious equation only by a convention you have to remember, and nothing stops you writing `du[1]` twice. On the right `D(S) ~ -kappa*S*I` reads as the equation does, and the name `S` travels with the model, which is why the solution object can answer `sol[S]` later without you tracking that S was index one. The symbolic form is also what lets the library differentiate the model, simplify it, or convert it to another kind of process — none of which it can do with a function whose body it cannot see. That is the trade: you give up nothing in speed, because the macro generates a kernel like the one on the left. ::: ## The same model, two toolkits {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="54%"} ::: {#cell-ch04-mtk .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using JumpProcesses @named jumpsys = JumpSystem( [MassActionJump(κ, [S => 1, I => 1], [S => -1, I => 1]; scale_rates = false), MassActionJump(γ, [I => 1], [I => -1, R => 1]; scale_rates = false)], t, [S, I, R], [κ, γ]) ``` ::: {#ch04-mtk .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Parameters (2): see parameters(jumpsys)

``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="46%"} ::: {#cell-ch04-catalyst .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Catalyst sir_network = @reaction_network begin κ, S + I --> 2I γ, I --> R end ``` ::: {#ch04-catalyst .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Model ##ReactionSystem#288:
Unknowns (3): see unknowns(##ReactionSystem#288)

Parameters (2): see parameters(##ReactionSystem#288)

``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: Who must be present sets the propensity; what the event does sets the state change. Catalyst reads both off the arrow. ::: {.notes} Read the two columns against each other rather than line by line. On the left you say the two lists explicitly: `[S => 1, I => 1]` is why the propensity is a product, `[S => -1, I => 1]` is the stoichiometric change vector. On the right the arrow says both at once — that is the whole saving, and it is why a reaction list stays readable at fifty reactions where a jump list does not. One rate constant per transition, so the beta-c-S-I-over-N from this morning becomes kappa-S-I with kappa equal to beta c over N. R nought is still 2. The book chapter uses kappa from here on. ::: ## Equivalent, to the last event {.smaller} ::: {#cell-ch04-equivalence .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using StableRNGs start = [S => 990, I => 10, R => 0, κ => 0.05*10/1000, γ => 0.25] mtk_path = solve(JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0); rng = StableRNG(3001)), SSAStepper()) catalyst_path = solve(JumpProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0], (0.0, 40.0), [:κ => 0.05*10/1000, :γ => 0.25]; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(3001)), SSAStepper()) mtk_path(grid, idxs = I) == catalyst_path(grid, idxs = sir_network.I) ``` ::: {#ch04-equivalence .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` true ``` ::: ::: Not merely similar — given the same seed, the same sequence of events. ::: {.notes} This is the slide that earns the word "equivalent". Both toolkits build the same two mass-action jumps, hand them to the same Direct aggregator, and draw from the same seeded stream, so the paths agree event for event, not just in distribution. Lowered to ODEs instead, the two peaks agree to about 1e-16, which is floating-point noise. If a comparison like this ever came out false you would have found a real bug in one of the two descriptions, so it is worth running. ::: ## Which toolkit, and when? {.smaller} | | ModelingToolkit.jl | Catalyst.jl | |---|---|---| | You describe | variables, equations, jumps | reactions | | Stoichiometry | written out per jump | read off the arrow | | Rate laws | any expression you write | mass action by default | | Covers | ODEs, SDEs, jumps, DAEs, control | reaction networks | | Comes with | structural simplification | network and conservation analysis | | Reach for it when | the model is not a reaction network | it is | Neither is a wrapper around the other, and neither is the "advanced" one. The question is only whether your model is naturally a set of reactions. ::: {.notes} The honest summary: if you can draw your model as arrows between boxes, Catalyst will say it in fewer lines and give you network analysis for free. Ageing, waning, vaccination schedules and contact matrices are all still reactions, so that covers most of epidemiology. The moment you want a term that is not a reaction — a delay, an optimal control, a mass-matrix constraint — you are in ModelingToolkit, and Catalyst systems convert into it anyway. Do not let anyone leave thinking they must pick one. The worksheet this afternoon uses ModelingToolkit because jumps are the topic; the reaction networks session later in the week is entirely Catalyst. ::: ## One `solve`, two processes {.smaller} ::: {#cell-ch04-dispatch .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ode_problem = ODEProblem(complete(odesys), start, (0.0, 40.0)) jump_problem = JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0); rng = StableRNG(3001)) ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5()) # deterministic jump_solution = solve(jump_problem, SSAStepper()) # one exact path (ode = round(maximum(ode_solution[I]); digits = 1), jump = maximum(jump_solution[I])) ``` ::: {#ch04-dispatch .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (ode = 157.6, jump = 201.0) ``` ::: ::: Different problem, different solver — but `solve`, `sol[I]` and `sol(grid)` are the same words in both cases. ::: {.notes} This is the multiple-dispatch argument, made concrete rather than asserted. Everything that *differs* between a deterministic and a stochastic model is in how the problem is built: differential equations against jumps, Tsit5 against SSAStepper. Everything downstream is identical, because `solve` dispatches on the problem type and the solution object answers `sol[I]` the same way whichever process produced it. That is why the sensitivity, estimation and intervention sessions later in the week can reuse one set of habits across model types instead of learning a new interface each time. It is also why swapping a model class is usually a two-line change, not a rewrite. ::: ## Day 1: many runs, by hand {.smaller} One path tells you almost nothing, so we need twenty. Yesterday's answer was a comprehension: ::: {#cell-ch04-byhand .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Statistics run_once(seed) = solve( JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0); rng = StableRNG(seed)), SSAStepper())(grid, idxs = I) paths_by_hand = [run_once(3000 + k) for k in 1:20] (runs = length(paths_by_hand), mean_peak = round(mean(maximum.(paths_by_hand)); digits = 1)) ``` ::: {#ch04-byhand .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (runs = 20, mean_peak = 177.7) ``` ::: ::: You wrote the loop, the seeding and the storage — and nothing here says the runs are independent, so nothing exploits it. ::: {.notes} Nothing is wrong with this code and everybody has written it. Point at what it costs: three decisions you had to make and get right, none of which are about epidemiology. Where do seeds come from, so runs are reproducible and not identical. What shape do you store results in. And who computes the summary. The deeper problem is the last clause on the slide. A comprehension is a sequential instruction, so the fact that twenty independent epidemics could run on twenty cores is information you have and the machine does not. ::: ## `EnsembleProblem`: declare the runs {.smaller} ::: {#cell-ch04-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} jump_at(seed) = JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0); rng = StableRNG(seed)) ensemble = EnsembleProblem(jump_at(3001); prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> jump_at(3000 + ctx.sim_id)) runs = solve(ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories = 20) length(runs.u) ``` ::: {#ch04-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 20 ``` ::: ::: `prob_func` says how trajectory `ctx.sim_id` differs — here, its seed. The number of runs moves out of the code and into the call. ::: {.notes} Read it as a description rather than a loop. The ensemble problem says *what a trajectory is*; `trajectories = 20` says how many you want; `EnsembleThreads()` says who runs them. Change twenty to twenty thousand and no code changes. `prob_func` is the hook that matters. Here it only varies the seed, which is the pure stochastic-replication case: same model, same parameters, different random stream. Give it a different parameter instead and the identical machinery becomes a parameter sweep, which is exactly what the sensitivity session does on Thursday with Latin hypercube samples. One interface, two uses. Say the thing about seeding explicitly: without `prob_func` every trajectory would share one random stream, which is a genuine trap under threading. ::: ## Twenty paths and the ODE {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch04-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch04-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Twenty CTMC paths of infectious prevalence with the mean-field ODE. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Five minutes, and let them look before you talk. Two things to point at. First the spread in *timing*: every path has the same shape but peaks somewhere between roughly day 12 and day 23. Second, and this is the one worth labouring: the dashed ODE is not the average of the paths. Its peak is near 158 while the mean of the twenty individual peak heights is around 178, because each path peaks at its own time and averaging asynchronous peaks flattens the curve. So "the ODE peak" and "the average peak of an epidemic" are different quantities. The three numbers in the title are the previous slide made concrete: sd is the epidemics varying, se is how well twenty runs pin the average down. Note that none of these twenty paths fades out. With ten initial infectives and $R_0=2$ that is expected, since fade-out needs all ten introductions to fail. Fade-out is a small-introduction phenomenon, and the worksheet quantifies it. ::: ## Summaries without a summariser {.center .smaller} ```julia summary = EnsembleSummary(runs, grid) # mean and quantiles, per variable ``` ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch05-band .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch05-band .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Mean infectious prevalence over the same twenty paths with a 5th-95th percentile band, against the mean-field ODE. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} `EnsembleSummary` is the reason the previous slide stored nothing by hand: mean and quantiles across trajectories, on a grid the trajectories do not share, because each one stops at its own last event. Now compare the two curves in the title. The ensemble mean peaks lower than the individual paths did on the last slide — averaging asynchronous peaks flattens them — and it is *still* not the ODE. The band is the honest picture: wide around the peak, where timing varies most, and narrow at both ends where every path agrees. If you only ever plot a mean, you have thrown that away. ::: ## What exactness costs {.smaller} Every event is simulated individually, so the work is set by the *event count*, not by the time horizon. One counting kernel answers both questions: ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function count_events(N, I₀, β, c, γ, tmax, rng; sis = false) t, S, I, n = 0.0, N - I₀, I₀, 0 while t < tmax && I > 0 infection = β*c*S*I/N a₀ = infection + γ*I t += randexp(rng)/a₀ t > tmax && break if rand(rng)*a₀ < infection S -= 1; I += 1 else I -= 1; sis && (S += 1) end n += 1 end n end ``` ::: Timed over `N` from $10^3$ to $10^7$ with 1% initially infected, and — with `sis = true`, so recovery returns to susceptible — over rising contact rates. ::: {.notes} The kernel allocates nothing and is written the obvious way — no vectorisation, no rewriting in C. That is the "Julia is fast" claim from this morning made concrete: ten million events in a scalar loop is a reasonable thing to do here. ::: ## Cost grows with size and with rates {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch05-cost .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch05-cost .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Left: wall-clock time for one exact SIR path against population size, log-log, with a slope-one reference. Right: event count for an SIS model at N = 10⁵ as the contact rate rises. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Two different reasons to be slow. Size is the obvious one: each individual is moved through the system one event at a time, so the count comes out at about 1.55N here and the slope-one reference confirms the cost is linear in N. Rates are the subtler one. In a closed SIR the event count can never exceed 2N, because every individual is infected at most once — so raising the contact rate only pushes you towards the final-size bound. Allow reinfection and that ceiling goes: events then accumulate at roughly 2*gamma*I(t), so cost is driven by endemic prevalence, which rises with the contact rate. Crossing the threshold from c = 5 (R0 = 1) to c = 10 (R0 = 2) multiplies the work about thirty-fold. It does not grow without limit, though: prevalence saturates towards N, so the curve flattens off at roughly 2*gamma*N*tmax, which is 2e6 events here. The honest summary is that exact simulation costs one step per event, and the event count is what you have to reason about. That is where tau-leaping and hybrid methods earn their place. ::: ## Takeaways - Propensities determine both waiting times and event probabilities. - Two notations, one process: ModelingToolkit and Catalyst give the same events. - `EnsembleProblem` declares the replicates; `prob_func` seeds them. - Exact jumps preserve integer states and population conservation. - Ensemble summaries are needed for comparison with an ODE. - Exactness is paid for per event, so cost follows the event count. ::: {.notes} Invite readers to open the Pluto companion and change transmission or the initial number infected. The book contains the random time-change derivation and exercises. :::
